input.question: Salts are constantly added to the ocean through volcanic emissions, runoff from continents, and the weathering of rocks in general, but is there any process that reverses this and removes it?
input.ground_truth: Yes. Salt can settle out, be captured by organic processes, and (most commonly) become landlocked. In that last one, a part of the ocean recedes or gets cut off from the rest of the ocean. The water evaporates and deposits the salt (which gets buried over time), then the fresh water rains back into the rest of the ocean.

Question: Salts are constantly added to the ocean through volcanic emissions, runoff from continents, and the weathering of rocks in general, but is there any process that reverses this and removes it?

response.prediction:
Sure! Imagine the ocean is like a big bathtub. Every day, we put more and more salt in it—some comes from volcanoes, some from the ground when it rains, and some from rocks breaking apart. But if we kept putting salt in and never took any out, the bathtub would get too salty to swim in!

Luckily, the Earth has ways to take some salt out of the ocean. One way is when the water in the ocean evaporates (turns into vapor and goes up into the sky), but the salt stays behind. Over a long, long time, this makes the ocean a little bit less salty in some places. Also, sometimes salty water gets pushed deep into the ground, where it can stay for a very long time. So, even though we keep adding salt, the Earth finds ways to take some of it away!
